html:
The Baikal-Amur Mainline, or BAM, is a railway of about 4,300 kilometres across eastern Siberia, running north of Lake Baikal to the Pacific coast. It lies several hundred kilometres north of the older Trans-Siberian Railway.

Work first began in the 1930s with Gulag prisoners, but it stopped during the Second World War and the rails were torn up for use elsewhere. In 1974 Leonid Brezhnev relaunched it as the "construction project of the century". Young volunteers of the Komsomol, the Communist youth league, came from across the Soviet Union, lured by high pay and adventure.

The route crossed permafrost, swamps, earthquake zones and mountain ranges that needed long tunnels. The line was declared joined in 1984, but full service took years more, and the longest tunnel was only finished in 2003. It was meant to open up Siberia's minerals and to give a second route to the Pacific, away from the Chinese border after the Sino-Soviet split. Its great cost made it a symbol of late Soviet stagnation.
